title: Food in Idioms
text:
Food words appear in idioms across many languages, reflecting what communities ate and valued. To have bread and butter means to have a basic livelihood, while to be a piece of cake describes something easy. Such expressions preserve a record of daily life, showing which foods were central to survival and comfort.

Yet the connection between an idiom and its food is not always simple. Some scholars argue that a phrase borrowed from another culture may have changed its meaning in translation. Others note that repeated use can strip a metaphor of its original image, so speakers use it without picturing any bread or cake at all.

questions.text: According to paragraph one, what does 'to have bread and butter' mean?
According to paragraph two, what can happen to a phrase borrowed from another culture?
options: It always stays exactly the same
It may change its meaning in translation

questions.text: What can be inferred about the connection between idioms and their food origins?
options: It is only found in cookbooks

questions.text: What does the writer suggest happens after repeated use of a metaphor?
options: Speakers may use it without picturing the original image

paragraph_translations: تظهر كلمات الطعام في تعابير كثيرة عبر لغات متعددة، تعكس ما كانت تأكله المجتمعات وما تقدّره. فالقول to have bread and butter يعني امتلاك مصدر رزق أساسي، بينما يصف القول to be a piece of cake شيئاً سهلاً. وتحفظ هذه التعابير سجلاً للحياة اليومية، وتبيّن أي الأطعمة كانت محورية للبقاء والراحة.

لكن الصلة بين التعبير وطعامه ليست دائماً بسيطة. يرى بعض الباحثين أن عبارة مستعارة من ثقافة أخرى قد تغيّر معناها عند الترجمة. ويلاحظ آخرون أن الاستعمال المتكرر قد يجرّد الاستعارة من صورتها الأصلية، فيستعملها المتكلمون دون أن يتخيلوا خبزاً أو كعكة على الإطلاق.
